data.title: The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Foundayo, Wegovy pill keep climibing
data.description:
With the recent launches of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo, the obesity market has started to shift toward oral GLP-1 drugs. While Novo leverages its first-mover advantage with the familiar Wegovy brand, Lilly is betting that the freedom from strict fasting and water requirements can give Foundayo an edge.

Each week, Fierce Pharma’s Oral GLP-1 Tracker will leverage analysts’ notes and IQVIA data to monitor prescription trends and shifting market shares as these two titans vie to become the go-to oral weight-loss solution for millions.

Nov. 13, 2026 

Over the last week, oral obesity medicines continued their upward trajectory, with both Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill scripts climbing to new heights.  

Foundayo, in its 31st week since launch, saw its best uptake yet with 69K scripts—a  7% week-over-week jump—according to notes from Citi and Jefferies citing data from IQVIA. But Lilly’s oral option is still well behind Novo’s Wegovy pill launch pace, which hit 163K scripts at week 31 of its own rollout.  

According to Jeffries, Foundayo is now making up for roughly 40% of new oral obesity prescriptions and 45% of the U.S. oral market's incremental growth. Meanwhile, competition between the two metabolic rivals is expanding geographically as Lilly and Novo continue to launch their obesity pills into new markets.  

For Novo’s part, week 42 of the Wegovy pill launch saw prescriptions climb slightly to 185K. Jeffries attributed a 72.8% overall oral market share to the Danish pharma’s pill, with Foundayo holding the remaining 27.2%. 

Nov. 6, 2026

Heading into Halloween weekend, both Novo and Lilly saw scripts for their oral obesity medicines tick up. 

In its 30th launch week, Lilly’s Foundayo racked up roughly 65K prescriptions, seemingly topping a record of more than 64K scripts set in week 25 of the rollout, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. Still, the medicine’s performance pales in comparison to Novo’s Wegovy pill at week 30 of its own launch, when the semaglutide tablet reeled in roughly 173K scripts. 

For the last weekly period, the Wegovy pill charted a 0.5% script increase—or around 8K new prescriptions—to land at around 184K total. That’s roughly on par with the height of the pill’s script performance in 2026 so far and marked a rebound from roughly 183K the prior week. 

Novo reported earlier this week that the Wegovy pill generated 5.39 billion Danish kroner (nearly $811 million) in third-quarter sales. Over the same period, Lilly reported $184 million in sales of Foundayo. 

On an analyst call, Novo’s EVP of U.S. operations, Jamey Millar, resurfaced caveats with the data IQVIA is using to track the oral GLP-1 launches, arguing that Novo boasts “a much more extensive ecosystem of partners for Wegovy” than Lilly, and that those partners “don’t report to IQVIA in absolute terms.” 

“So we’ve consistently seen a lower capture rate for Wegovy pill than the competitive oral product,” he suggested. 

Based on the latest weekly metrics, Lilly holds a little more than a 26% share of the overall oral obesity market compared to Novo’s nearly 74%, the Jefferies team said in its note. 

UPDATED: Oct. 30, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill ticked back up last week, although neither matched previous records.

Foundayo enjoyed 63,110 total scripts in its 29th week of launch, still shy of its 64,268-script record set in week 25, according IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

The Wegovy pill's roughly 183K scripts also came slightly below the 184K height it had briefly reached five weeks ago. During the week, the oral version of Novo's obesity med constituted 36% of all Wegovy scripts.

Approximately 4 in 10 patients starting an oral obesity medicine choose Foundayo, and the number of new Foundayo patients in the third quarter doubled from the previous quarter, Lilly's CFO said on the company's Q3 earnings call Thursday.

In Q3, Foundayo sales reached $184 million, including $124 million from the U.S., missing consensus estimates by $50 million, according to a Jefferies note. Still, Lilly's stock price jumped during Thursday's earnings report, "which to us suggests investors are increasingly focusing on the breadth and depth of [Lilly]'s obesity franchise rather than near-term Foundayo [numbers]," Jefferies' analysts said. Sales from both of Lilly's tirzepatide products, Mounjaro and Zepbound, came in above Wall Street's projections during Q3.

UPDATED: Oct. 23, 2026

Last week’s federal holiday, Columbus Day, led to an unsurprising dip for prescriptions of both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 rival Foundayo in the U.S. 

In the prior-week reporting period, Novo’s Wegovy pill saw prescriptions fall slightly to around 173K versus the 173.5K tallied the week ending Oct. 9, according to Citi and Jefferies analysts, both of whom leverage prescribing data from IQVIA. 

For that same period, prescriptions of Eli Lilly’s GLP-1 pill Foundayo slipped around 4% week over week to 58K. 

The minor reversal for both drugs shouldn’t come as a surprise, given that national holidays are liable to impact weekly prescribing trends. 

Looking at the broader oral GLP-1 market, Lilly’s share presently sits a little higher than 25%, according to the Jefferies team, while Novo holds a nearly 75% piece of the pie. 

Meanwhile, as Novo and Lilly vie over the ever-important U.S. obesity market, the GLP-1 opportunity taking shape across other massive countries like China, India and Brazil could grow from $6.6 billion now to a whopping $22 billion by the middle of the next decade, according to a new J.P. Morgan estimate reported by Reuters Friday. 

UPDATED: Oct. 16, 2026

The previous week was rather uneventful for the two oral GLP-1 drugs as Americans geared up for another national holiday, Columbus Day.

Total prescriptions for Novo's Wegovy pill dipped about 3% sequentially to approximately 173.5K last week. Again, the script number was the result of a compromise between Citi's reported 173K and Jefferies' 174K, both referencing IQVIA.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo scripts ticked up about 4% to 60,151, still shy of the small molecule's previous record of 64,268.

In the broader obesity market, Lilly's Zepbound remained the leader with about 801.8K total scripts, relatively flat week over week. All Wegovy scripts across its injectable and oral forms trended 2.5% downward and landed at about 492.6K, according to Citi.

Earlier this week, drug regulators at the European Medicines Agency recommended a marketing authorization in the European Union for Foundayo for both weight management and Type 2 diabetes in adults. The European Commission is expected to sign off on the approval in a few weeks. 

UPDATED: Oct. 9, 2026

Prescriptions for Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill pulled back a little during the last week. 

In its 26th week of launch, Foundayo achieved 57,920 total scripts, down 9.9% sequentially, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

For oral Wegovy, Citi said IQVIA recorded roughly 179K scripts, while Jefferies quoted 180K. To reconcile the discrepancy between the two numbers, we used 179.5K, which translates into a 1.4% weekly decline.

In fact, scripts for all major GLP-1s declined last week across diabetes and obesity care, save for Lilly's Zepbound KwikPen, a prefilled injection pen that delivers four fixed weekly doses of tirzepatide, according to Jefferies. Overall Zepbound scripts dipped below 800K in a 0.8% decrease sequentially, just as Novo's total Wegovy scripts fell 2.7% to 505.5K, according to Citi.

Based on the numbers, Jefferies now models $208 million for Foundayo sales in the third quarter, which the team noted is in line with consensus.

UPDATED: Oct. 2, 2026

Eli Lilly's Foundayo is showing clearer signs of acceleration. Total prescriptions for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist surged about 21% to 64,268 during last week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. That haul came off a 13% sequential increase the week before that.

"We're seeing early signs of growth in Q3 for Foundayo," Jefferies analysts wrote in an Oct. 2 note.

Recent expansion of Foundayo could be attributed to a direct-to-consumer ad first aired in late August featuring Martha Stewart, as well as the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program which, as of July, offers eligible seniors GLP-1 obesity drugs at a $50 monthly copay.

Meanwhile, Novo's Wegovy pill scripts appear stuck at just above $180K. Except for a Labor Day holiday lull, total weekly scripts for the oral semaglutide product have hovered between 181K and 184K over the past five weeks, including 182K last week, according to Citi.

It's worth noting that Foundayo took 25 weeks to reach what the Wegovy pill achieved in just seven weeks in terms of total scripts. But the gap between the two drugs is closing. As Jefferies noted, Lilly owned 26% of the oral obesity market as of last week, versus a little less than 23% in the previous two weeks.

Overall, Lilly's Zepbound remains the obesity market leader with total scripts of 805.7K, up 2.3% sequentially, according to Citi. Novo's total Wegovy scripts for the pill and the injectable were down 0.6% sequentially to a 519.6K.

At the European Association for the Study of Diabetes annual meeting in Milan earlier this week, both Lilly and Novo rolled out multiple data sets touting the blood-sugar, weight-loss, cardiovascular benefits of their GLP-1 programs amid a wave of potential challengers.

UPDATED: Sept. 25, 2026

Total prescriptions for both Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill have bounced back following a holiday dip and reached new records. Weekly scripts for the Wegov pill jumped 14% sequentially to about 184K, compared with its previous high of 183K, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. Foundayo climbed 13% to cross 50K for the first time, reaching 53,321.

Foundayo now captures about 1 out of 3 new starts for oral GLP-1 obesity drugs, and “that’s growing week over week,” Lilly CEO David Ricks told CNBC in an interview this week. 

As Leerink Partners analysts noted in a Sept. 23 note, effective Sept. 1, Lilly cut the initial-dose pricing for Foundayo 0.8 mg, 2.5 mg and 5.5 mg to $149, $149 and $199 per month for self-pay patients, respectively. The company framed the promotion as an elasticity experiment and as a push to the first maintenance dose, according to the Leerink note.

As Jefferies analysts pointed out in a Sept. 25 note, the majority of Foundayo scripts seem to be cash pay, with about 80% of patients still on starting doses.

Based on the IQVIA data so far, the Jefferies team estimated U.S. Foundayo revenues of $203 million in the third quarter, slightly lower than the $209 million consensus projection. 

Broadly speaking, Lilly yielded 0.6 percentage point of its obesity market share to Novo during the previous week, but still maintained its share level above 60%, according to Citi. 

In the recently launched Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, Lilly is capturing 7 out of 10 patients, with many on its Zepbound, Ricks told CNBC. Foundayo, according to Ricks, is attracting Medicare patients looking for convenience but not necessarily a huge weight-loss effect. 

UPDATED: Sept. 18, 2026

As expected, the past U.S. Labor Day holiday took a toll on obesity drugs' prescription numbers. According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, weekly scripts for Novo's Wegovy pill dropped roughly 12% sequentially to about 161K for the last week. The decline for Foundayo was modest, at just 1%, as the Lilly drug still managed to rake in more than 47K scripts. 

Lilly this week said Foundayo captured more than 30% of new patients in the U.S. market for oral obesity ​treatments, Reuters reported. 

Citing Bloomberg Symphony data, Jefferies analysts suggested in a Friday note that Foundayo's recent acceleration "has been driven primarily by retail/commercial channels."

Elsewhere, Lilly's total Zepbound scripts were down 8.5% week over week, but the GIP/GLP-1 drug expanded its market share by 0.4% versus Novo's Wegovy franchise, whose scripts decreased 10% during the period.

UPDATED: Sept. 11, 2026

Both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo saw their highest total prescriptions so far over the past week as the companies’ oral obesity battle continues to play out.  

According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, the Wegovy pill reached an approximate 183K total scripts for the most recent reporting period, versus 181K the week prior. Foundayo, for its part, climbed nearly 8% to reach 47.5K scripts. Citi analysts emphasized that IQVIA may still be missing some Foundayo prescriptions made through telehealth channels. 

Meanwhile, using the last four weeks as a guide, total GLP-1 prescriptions have increased by 5.4%, compared to a 6.8% decline the prior year, the Citi team said. Citi analysts attributed the 12-percentage-point swing to the expansion of oral GLP-1 therapies, which is likely broadening access to the class and drawing in new patients.  

Across the broader landscape, Lilly’s tirzepatide currently holds a nearly 57% share of the total GLP-1 market, compared to around 49.5% last year, while Novo’s semaglutide has stayed relatively flat at a 37% share, the analysts added.  

UPDATED: Sept. 4, 2026

Total prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo both grew over the past week, reaching roughly 181K (+3%) and 44K (+8%), IQVIA data showed, as cited by Citi. Both numbers are the two meds' highest so far. 

While Foundayo has yet to catch up with the Wegovy pill, the market share gap between the two oral drugs is slowly narrowing. According to an Aug. 28 Jefferies note based on data the previous week, Foundayo's share of new prescriptions (NRx), which exclude refills, was 21.5% in the oral obesity market.

Back to the most recent week, the Wegovy pill's position within the Wegovy family remained stable at 35%, as total Wegovy scripts increased 2.7% sequentially to 513.5K. During the same period, Lilly's Zepbound scripts climbed 1.6% to a little fewer than 772K.  

UPDATE: Aug. 28, 2026

Twenty weeks into its launch, Eli Lilly's Foundayo has finally exceeded 40,000 in weekly prescriptions, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 drug posted 40,862 scripts last week, bouncing back from a small dip the week prior. Still, the drug's scripts level is no match for the roughly 57K that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill garnered at week 6 of its own launch.

In its 33rd week of launch, the Wegovy pill booked roughly 175K scripts, slightly down from 176K, per IQVIA. The share of the oral version of semaglutide in all Wegovy obesity scripts was flat week over week at 35%. All told, across the pill and the injectable, Wegovy's weekly scripts were a little over 500K, down 0.8% sequentially.

As Jefferies analysts observed in an Aug. 21 note, Wegovy has been relatively flat since the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program began July 1.

Overall, the roughly 60%-40% obesity market share split between Lilly and Novo remained stable, as Lilly's Zepbound held its ground as the most popular drug.

UPDATE: Aug. 21, 2026

After a one-week hiccup, Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill regained its momentum last week with its largest prescription rate since it was launched in January. There were more than 176,000 prescriptions for the pill in the period, according to data gathered by IQVIA and cited in a note by Citi. 

The oral treatment now accounts for 35% of total Wegovy prescriptions, which is up from 33% the previous week, analysts from Citi said in their weekly update to investors.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo, which had been on a steady five-week climb, backtracked, with a drop-off from 38,928 prescriptions in the prior period to 36,620 in the latest week.

The movements for the two oral treatments contributed to overall market share adjustments for the companies' diabetes and obesity medicines. While Lilly made a 0.1% gain to 56.7%, Novo increased its market share by 0.3% to 37.1%.  

UPDATE: Aug. 14, 2026

Despite its leading position in the oral GLP-1 market, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill seems to be hitting a market share ceiling. For months now, shares of total prescriptions for Wegovy pill within the entire Wegovy franchise have struggled to break through the one-third mark.

While share of oral semaglutide within all Wegovy scripts hit 35% in our previous update, it fell back to 33% last week, as Wegovy pill scripts dropped to about 163K, down from a high of roughly 172K the week prior, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

Total Wegovy scripts, including the original injectable, declined 1.1% sequentially to about 495.5K. As a result, Novo yielded about 0.7 percentage point in obesity market share to Eli Lilly's Zepbound last week based on the IQVIA data. The split stood at 39.9% and 60.1% between Novo and Lilly.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo continued its upward trajectory with 38,928 total scripts, representing another step up from its previous record of 34,219 set the week prior.

UPDATE: Aug. 7, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo continue to build, jumping 16% sequentially to 34,219 the previous week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 med has been on a roll lately as it appears to celebrate four weeks of consecutive growth in total scripts. However, as Citi noted, there's still a potential gap in IQVIA's capture of telehealth data, and it's not clear how much of the scripts growth was from IQVIA getting better at including those data, or, if the actual growth was much faster in telehealth channels.

This week, Lilly's reported Foundayo sales for the second quarter—$98 million in total, including $67 million in the U.S.—disappointed many. As CEO David Ricks noted on an earnings call, Lilly began broad direct-to-consumer marketing to raise consumer awareness after securing commercial access across the three major pharmacy benefit managers in June. Besides, The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program went live on July 1, offering coverage for certain weight-loss medications, including Foundayo, for a $50 copayment per month. Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, said the company is "starting to see an inflection point on Foundayo now."

As for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill, total scripts recorded by IQVIA have been largely flat with small upticks in the past two weeks, having reached roughly 172K in the previous week. The oral version of semaglutide now makes up 35% of total Wegovy scripts, which take up about 40.6% of the U.S. obesity market share, as Lilly's Zepbound remains the leader. 

UPDATE: July 31, 2026

The small inflection point we noticed two weeks ago regarding Eli Lilly's Foundayo does not appear to be a flash in the pan. Weekly total prescriptions for the small molecule reached 29,388, a new high for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist after three weeks of consecutive growth, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

As IQVIA may be missing some scripts from telehealth channels, we will get a clearer picture of Foundayo's launch progress when Lilly reports its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday, Aug. 5. Analysts at Jefferies have been modeling $71 million in U.S. sales for the quarter based on IQVIA data.

Meanwhile, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill remains far ahead in the oral GLP-1 race with total scripts also hitting a new record of about 171,700, according to Citi. The number represents 1.1% growth from its previous best recorded during the prior week.

Coincidentally, the entire GLP-1 class also saw its total scripts grow 1.1% sequentially across diabetes and obesity uses. Lilly's Zepbound regained some lost ground with total scripts up 1.9% week over week. That's compared to Wegovy, which now makes up 40.6% of the obesity market after a 0.2% sequential decline in total scripts. 

Novo reports earnings on the same day as Lilly, Aug. 5.

UPDATE: July 24, 2026

After a post-holiday lull, prescriptions for GLP-1s have more than bounced back. Weekly prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo reached new highs during the previous week, collecting 169,800 and 26,760, respectively, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The two oral drugs' previous records were about 161.5K and 24.3K, respectively. 

Other GLP-1 drugs also enjoyed a boost, as total GLP-1 scripts across obesity and diabetes increased 6.6% sequentially, according to Citi.

From the obesity front, scripts for Lilly's Zepbound rose 7.7% sequentially to about 710K. The GLP-1/GIP dual agonist conceded 0.6 percentage points of market share to Novo but remains ahead of the game with a 58.9% share. That's compared to a 10.5% week-over-week scripts expansion for Novo's Wegovy, which mounted to about 495.5K. In that basket, about 34% belonged to Wegovy pill.

UPDATE: July 17, 2026

Following the Independence Day holiday, the overall GLP-1 market was down 5.1% week over week as measured by total prescriptions across obesity and diabetes uses, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi.

In the obesity field specifically, total scripts for Eli Lilly's Zepbound shrank by 3.1% sequentially to a little below 660K, while Novo Nordisk's Wegovy dipped 4.4% to about 448.5K.

Against this backdrop, Lilly's oral Foundayo seemed to enjoy a small inflection point, with a total 24,303 scripts notably breaking away from its roughly 20K level in the prior five weeks.  

Meanwhile, joining the bigger trend, Wegovy pill scripts dropped to 147.5K during the week, versus about 153K the prior week or 161.5K at its peak. But the contribution of the oral version to the overall Wegovy scripts remained stable at around a third, per Citi's note. 

UPDATE: July 10, 2026

The launch of Eli Lilly’s Foundayo remains “muted,” with weekly prescriptions flat over the last five weeks, analysts from Jefferies said in a July 10 note. The analysis is based on data collected by IQVIA.

In the 13th week of Foundayo’s launch, IQVIA reported 19,550 prescriptions, down for the third straight week after peaking at Week 10 with 21,648 prescriptions. The figure also comes in significantly shy of the Week 13 launch of Novo’s Wegovy pill (more than 105K scripts) and Lilly’s injected obesity treatment Zepbound (59K), but ahead of Novo’s injected Wegovy (13K).

Meanwhile, weekly scripts for Wegovy pill ticked slightly upward sequentially to about 153K, although they still lag behind the drug’s peak of more than 161K.

Jefferies points out that CVS was the last of the big three PBMs to provide coverage of Foundayo, starting on June 1. By contrast, Wegovy had full coverage at the first week of its launch.

While Jefferies’ $71 million quarterly sales projection for Foundayo sits significantly below Wall Street consensus of $130 million, the team still believes that the Lilly med can reach the consensus revenue estimate of $1.2 billion for 2026.

UPDATE: July 6, 2026

For a month now, weekly prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo have been hovering at around 20,000. In other words, three months into its market debut, the non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist was still at the same script level that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill had achieved in two to three weeks post-launch.

For the week ended on June 26, Foundayo's total scripts dipped about 4% sequentially to 19,830, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. During the same period, scripts were also down about 2% for oral Wegovy, reaching about 149,000.

In a July 4 report, Jefferies analysts modeled about $71 million in U.S. sales during Foundayo's debut quarter from April to June, versus the team's previous estimate of $85 million in a June 26 report. Wall Street's consensus currently has the number at $130 million. To reach its estimate, Jefferies used an illustrative calculation based on the IQVIA data, with certain assumptions regarding pricing, dosing and stocking.

While Lilly still lags Novo on the oral GLP-1 battlefield, the Indianapolis pharma has maintained a majority 59.5% share of the overall obesity market, according to IQVIA's prescription data.  

As Novo's injectable Wegovy gained about 0.2% scripts (roughly 500) to reach 315,000 for the period, Lilly's Zepbound expanded by 1%, including 375,000 (+3,500) from Zepbound autoinjector and 289,000 (+2,000) from Zepbound DTC Vial+KwikPen.

UPDATE: June 29, 2026

Likely thanks to the Juneteenth federal holiday, prescriptions for both Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo were lower compared with their highest. For the week ended on June 19, Foundayo logged 20,594 total scripts, down from 21,648 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. 

For oral Wegovy, the numbers were about 152,000 for the June 19 week, a roughly 9,500 (5.9%) decrease from the prior week. 

As Jefferies' analysts noted, most GLP-1 scripts were down or rather flat in their weekly comparisons. Injectable Wegovy added about 1,000 (0.3%) scripts, landing at 315,000. Mounjaro essentially saw no change, at 804,000.

Lilly has previously noted that it takes time to build awareness for Foundayo as a new brand, whereas Novo benefits from familiarity with the Wegovy moniker. 

Meanwhile, Sandoz just announced that the FDA has accepted its generic tirzepatide autoinjector applications, covering all indications of Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound. We'll see how the availability of a generic injectable version shakes up the oral market. 

UPDATE: June 18, 2026

Name recognition and "familiarity" with Novo Nordisk's oral Wegovy has contributed to its rapid uptake in its battle with Lilly's oral GLP-1 Foundayo, according to Spherix analyst Jim Hickey, who conducts monthly surveys with doctors who prescribe the treatments. See Fierce's story on Hickey's analysis here.

UPDATE: June 12, 2026

The share of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill among total Wegovy scripts appears to have reached a plateau, hovering around one-third over the past few weeks. The latest number for the week ended on June 5 was 33%, compared with 30%, 32% and 31% in the prior weeks, according to Citi. 

Meanwhile, the obesity market share split between Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound has been relatively stable at around 40% to 42%, as the Indianapolis pharma's oral Foundayo makes up only a small portion of the market even though its own scripts continue to build. 

Wegovy's total scripts were up 9.8% on a weekly basis, reaching nearly 484,500. Within this haul, Wegovy pill contributed roughly 159,000, the oral version's highest since its launch. The drug's previous highest was 146,000 before dipping to 134,000 in our last update.

Zepbound's scripts also grew week over week by 9.3%, nearing 667,400 for the week. During the same period, IQVIA tracked slightly shy of 20,000 scripts from Foundayo in its ninth week on the market, compared with nearly 17,000 the prior week. 

Thanks to the expansion of the oral version, Wegovy overall now commands 42.1% of the obesity market. Tracing backwards, its share has been climbing steadily, clocking in at 41.9%, 41.2%, 41.4%, 40.5%, 40.4%, 42.6% and 40.4% in the past few weeks.

UPDATE: June 8, 2026

It took just over five months for Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill to log 3 million total U.S. prescriptions, underscoring “one of the strongest US pharmaceutical launches by volume on record,” the company announced in a June 7 press release. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s rival Foundayo has still yet to achieve more than 17,000 prescriptions, according to a June 5 note from Citi analysts.  

Using data from IQVIA, the analysts tracked 16,982 Foundayo prescriptions as of the drug's eighth week on the market since its April launch. However, the Citi team emphasizes that “there may be a gap in telehealth capture,” as Lilly has previously confirmed to the analysts around 20,000 Foundayo scripts since its launch. Foundayo has been floating around this range for several weeks now since hitting 16,698 at week six, the data show.

Meanwhile, Novo’s Wegovy pill was at 73,544 prescriptions by the time it had hit the same eight-week marker in its own launch. The drug had picked up one million prescriptions 12 weeks after launching and nabbed an additional two million prescriptions in the following ten weeks, Novo said in its release. At its three million total, one prescription is filled roughly every five seconds, the company pointed out in its release. 

Either way, IQVIA’s data suggests a preference for oral formulations in the wider GLP-1 market, with oral Wegovy prescriptions now contributing 30% of total Wegovy scripts, according to the Citi analysts. The oral offering may be driving a wider market for the obesity treatments as well, with Novo explaining in its recent release that more than 80% of its new prescriptions for the Wegovy pill come from people new to GLP-1 therapy. 

June 2 findings from Spherix Global Insights second the notion that oral GLP-1 pills are expanding the overall treatment pool and drawing in a “massive wave of new patients,” the company said in an emailed release. In oral Wegovy’s first four weeks on the market earlier this year, 73% of surveyed primary care physician reported prescribing the med, with over 98% who haven’t yet prescribed it planning to within the next six months, Spherix found. 

“Novo Nordisk’s early performance has set an exceptionally high bar for the competition,” Spherix’s gastroenterology franchise head, Jim Hickey, commented.

On a weekly basis, however, total GLP-1 prescriptions were trending downward over the week of June 1, falling 5.7% week-over-week, Citi analysts noted. Other than the continued rollout of Lilly and Novo’s respective weight loss pills, the analysts cited the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies as a key future event that they think could impact total prescriptions. 

UPDATE: June 1, 2026

In its seventh week on the market, which ended May 22, Eli Lilly’s obesity pill Foundayo continued to track below the pace of Novo Nordisk’s rival Wegovy pill at the same point in its launch.

At the same time, analysts at Jefferies and Citi again flagged caveats that could be skewing the numbers, with the Jefferies team espousing confidence that Lilly’s oral GLP-1 can still meet consensus sales projections for both the second quarter and 2026 as a whole. 

Breaking down the numbers, the Jefferies team put seventh-week total Foundayo prescriptions lower versus the previous week at roughly 11,700, with the clarification that the data’s source, IQVIA, had to use a “best-estimate” tally for the latest week’s prescription trends. 

That trend remains “numerically lower” than the course charted by Novo’s Wegovy pill, which racked up an impressive 67,000 prescriptions in its seventh week, although Foundayo’s performance still tracks ahead of Novo’s injectable Wegovy and Lilly’s first obesity incretin med Zepbound at the same point in their respective rollouts, the analyst team said. 

Lilly has suggested it expects the market for oral obesity meds to “develop over time” and has also cited the time needed to build new brand awareness for Foundayo, according to Jefferies, which added that the Lilly pill’s commercial reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly” compared to oral Wegovy. Lilly has confirmed that coverage of Foundayo through CVS Caremark, the United States’ biggest PBM, will begin this week. 

Despite those apparent growing pains, the analysts at Jefferies called Foundayo’s ability to meet consensus sales estimates in the near-term and for the full year as “doable.” The analysts currently predict that Lilly’s oral weight loss med will garner $145 million in the second quarter on the way to a $1.6 billion haul for the full year. 

Consensus estimates are tracking for Q2 and full-year Foundayo sales of $136 million and $1.2 billion, respectively, according to Jefferies. 

On that note, analysts at Citi, have repeatedly warned that IQVIA’s prescription data may be failing to account for telehealth referrals, citing comments from Lilly executives on the total patients they were tracking as of the company’s Q1 earnings call. For its part, Citi placed the total number of Foundayo scripts for the week ending May 22 at roughly 16,000, based on the IQVIA stats. 

By comparison, Novo’s Wegovy pill clocked some 146,000 total scripts over that same seven-day stretch, per Citi. Citi once more flagged that Novo’s Wegovy pill is making up a growing portion of overall semaglutide obesity prescriptions, which the team said points to “preferences for oral formulations.”

UPDATE: May 22, 2026

With both Novo Nordisk’s and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1s establishing their footing in the U.S. obesity market, the companies’ respective Wegovy pill and orforglipron tablet Foundayo are making their mark on prescription trends for a class previously confined primarily to injectables.

Looking at the past four weeks, total U.S. GLP-1 prescriptions were up 3.6%, compared to 1.8% at the same time last year, analysts at Citi wrote in a Friday note to clients, citing script tracking data from IQVIA. The Citi team attributed that momentum to the ability of Novo’s and Lilly’s new oral launches to “broaden and reshape the market” for obesity incretin drugs.

As of the week ended May 15, IQVIA logged nearly 17,000 prescriptions for Lilly’s Foundayo, which debuted on April 9. As in prior weeks, the Citi analysts caveated that IQVIA’s data may be missing key prescribing stats from telehealth channels, flagging Lilly executives’ comments during an earnings call at the end of last month that there were then roughly 20,000 patients on the new oral therapy.

Conversely, Novo’s Wegovy pill has recorded roughly 142,000 prescriptions as of last week, according to Citi’s note.

In an apparent sign of the new oral option's popularity, the analysts flagged that oral Wegovy now comprises 31% of total prescriptions for the brand, which is otherwise administered as an injection. The Citi team noted that this trend could signal “preferences for oral formulations.”

Meanwhile, scoping out the broader U.S. GLP-1 market over the past four weeks, Lilly’s tirzepatide brand—which includes both Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes—now holds a 54.8% share compared to a 47% piece of the pie last year. Novo’s U.S. market share for semaglutide has remained “relatively flat” over that stretch and clocked in at 37.4%, per Citi.

Week over week, total GLP-1 prescriptions were down a little less than 1% in the U.S. Looking at obesity specifically, Citi’s analysts flagged a 2.1% tirzepatide prescription decline versus last week, while Novo’s Wegovy prescriptions tracked at a positive 1.8%.

Aside from both companies' oral GLP-1 launches continuing to add texture to the market, the analysts noted that the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies on Novo’s and Lilly’s drugs could boost overall prescriptions for the class. 

UPDATE: May 15, 2026

Total prescriptions for Eli Lilly’s Foundayo reached 10,248 for the week that ended May 8, up from 7,335 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. While still on the rise, Foundayo’s growth pace continued to lag behind that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill during the same stage of their launch. 

Wegovy’s total scripts rose by 1.3% week over week to nearly 446,000, as its share in the obesity GLP-1 market climbed 0.1 percentage point to 40.5%, according to Citi.

However, Wegovy’s growth apparently didn’t come from its oral formulation. Wegovy pill scripts landed at about 137,000 for the week, down from roughly 143,000 the prior week, marking the first time that the pill's scripts have fallen since the oral launch in early January.

Scripts from the Wegovy pill made up 31% of total Wegovy scripts for the period, down 2 percentage points from the previous week. Still, Citi analysts argued that this roughly one-third of share “suggests preferences for oral formulations.”

Even as Wegovy gained ground, Lilly’s Zepbound remained the obesity market leader, with 59.5% share, as its nearly 656,000 scripts marked 0.8% growth week over week. 

UPDATE: May 8, 2026

As Eli Lilly’s Foundayo finds its footing on the market, Novo Nordisk’s own Wegovy pill—which got a three-month head start to launch over its rival this year—is starting to illuminate just how significant an oral GLP-1 may be to the lucrative obesity drug landscape. 

In the fourth week since its April 9 debut in the U.S., Lilly’s Foundayo has generated 7,335 total prescriptions, analysts at Citi wrote in a note to clients Friday, citing prescribing stats from IQVIA. 

That ramp-up looks slower on paper than that enjoyed by the Wegovy pill during its initial rollout, but the Citi team cautioned that there may be a gap in IQVIA data linked to telehealth prescriptions for Lilly’s tablet. They pointed to comments from Lilly executives late last week indicating that there were now some 20,000 patients on Foundayo, with the company noting that telehealth platforms were generating some 35% of the oral GLP-1 medicine’s current launch volume. 

The analysts acknowledged that Lilly’s early Foundayo prescription trends “continue to build,” while adding that they “look for further growth to develop the oral competitive market.” 

During its earnings call last week, Lilly added that upcoming coverage secured at major pharmacy benefit managers should come online by the middle of May, providing a likely sizeable tailwind to Foundayo’s trajectory. 

As for Novo, the company logged some 440,410 Wegovy prescriptions on the week that ended May 1, with oral Wegovy now making up 33% of those total obesity referrals, per the Citi analysts, who said that trend could reflect “preferences for oral formulations.”

The update on the oral obesity numbers comes after Novo earlier this week reported that the Wegovy pill generated 2.26 billion Danish kroner (around $355 million) in its first quarter on the U.S. market. 

For its part, Foundayo will likely need to start generating around 22,000 prescriptions a week in order to hit current consensus forecasts of $160 million in second-quarter sales, RBC Capital Markets’ Trung ​Huynh said this week, as cited by Reuters. 

UPDATE: May 4, 2026

With three weeks of data on Lilly’s oral GLP-1 launch in obesity now on the books, the dimensions of Foundayo’s rollout—and its critical comparison to that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill—are coming into focus. 

In its third week on the U.S. market, which ended April 24, Foundayo generated some 5,600 prescriptions, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a May 1 note to clients. That level of adoption is numerically lower than the stats recorded by the Wegovy pill in its third week, when prescriptions for the oral obesity med came in at around 26,100, per the note. 

Nevertheless, almost all of Foundayo’s recorded performance stems from cash pay channels, according to the Jefferies team, with commercial access via insurance set to come online by the middle of this month, which will likely give Foundayo a substantial boost in uptake. 

The team acknowledged that Foundayo’s reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly vs oral Wegovy’s.” 

Overall, the analysts described Foundayo as “off to a solid start,” and estimate the drug will generate $146 million in the second quarter and $1.6 billion for all of 2026. That compares to consensus forecasts of $134 million and $1.2 billion, respectively. 

Lilly told the Jefferies team that, as of week three of its launch, some 45% of Foundayo prescriptions were coming through its direct-to-patient channel LillyDirect, alongside 35% of referrals from telehealth providers and the remaining 20% coming from traditional retail venues. 

During an earnings call with analysts last week, Lilly executives noted that there were around 20,000 patients on Foundayo in the U.S. The drug was approved April 1. 

As for Novo’s pill, oral Wegovy lassoed around 135,000 total prescriptions during the week that ended April 24, according to the Jefferies notes. 

UPDATE: April 24, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 obesity treatment Foundayo has attracted 3,707 prescriptions though its second week on the market, lagging far behind the pace of Novo Nordisk’s GLP-1 pill Wegovy, which drew 18,410 prescriptions though its second week on the market in January. 

The results were made available by Jefferies from healthcare analytics firm IQVIA and are good through the week ending on April 17.

With the result, Lilly’s shares dipped by 4% on Friday, compared to a 7% gain for Novo.

Foundayo’s launch so far does compare favorably to that of Novo’s injected Wegovy, which numbered 1,578 prescriptions through two weeks when it reached the market in the U.S. but falls short of Lilly’s Zepbound pen, which counted 7,292 prescriptions through its second week.

In its note to investors, analysts from Jefferies called the result “disappointing vs. expectations."

Brand recognition has played a role, according to Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen, who said that online searches for GLP-1 drugs peaked during Wegovy’s launch, potentially boosting demand.

UPDATE: April 21, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo is off to a solid launch, drawing 1,390 prescriptions in its first week on the market, according to tracking figures from IQVIA and presented by Jefferies. The tabulation is from the week starting April 6. This compares to the 3,071 prescriptions Novo Nordisk garnered during its Wegovy pill launch week in January.

While Foundayo came up short in this oral GLP-1 launch week comparison, it did exceed the number of prescriptions recorded in the first week of the launch of both Lilly’s injected Zepbound (1,100) and Novo’s injected version of Wegovy (768).

In a note to clients, analysts with Jefferies cautioned that comparisons can be “tricky” given that oral Wegovy was launched at the start of the year and that initial capture rates from IQVIA are “volatile” and may not include product sampling. 

“Overall, we think Foundayo’s initial scripts look excellent,” the Jefferies team wrote, adding that it is modeling Foundayo’s sales to reach $1.6 billion this year, compared to a consensus of $1.5 billion, with its peak annual sales topping out at $30 billion versus the consensus of $26 billion. 

“We think the real opportunity for Foundayo is ex-U.S., given its clear advantages on scale, distribution and [cost of goods sold],” Jefferies wrote.

data.title: Sanofi teams with the Beano for Type 1 diabetes education push
data.description:
Sanofi’s U.K. business is partnering up with British comic stalwart the Beano once again to help British schools boost awareness of Type 1 diabetes. 

The Beano first came out in the U.K. back in 1938 but became a real mainstay in British culture from the 1950s onward. It features the adventures of Dennis (formerly Dennis the Menace) and his dog Gnasher, as well as a whole host of characters with a uniquely British and often rebellious sense of humor. 

Sanofi UK, as part of its campaigning for World Diabetes Day on Nov. 14, has chosen the Beano as part of its efforts to work in schools. 

Working also with DigiBete, an online and app-based resource for Type 1 diabetes, Sanofi and Beano are launching free primary school classroom resources to help teachers explain the condition.

Related

Sanofi runs emotive RSV campaign zeroing in on a baby’s bronchiolitis breathing sounds

Unlike Type 2 diabetes, which is more likely to be linked to adults and typically associated with other comorbidities such as obesity, Type 1 diabetes (T1D)—when the immune system attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas—is not linked to diet or lifestyle. It can be genetic but can also develop with no family history. 

The condition is often diagnosed in younger children with major peaks around ages four to six years old and 10 to 14—though it can develop and be diagnosed at any age. 

In the U.K., around 400,000 people are living with T1D, of which around 30,000 people are aged 18 years or younger. 

The “Beano for Schools” program uses the well-known world of Beano to help children “learn about both the biological and emotional impact of living with T1D, while encouraging greater understanding of an often ‘unseen condition,'” Sanofi said in a release.

The idea is that this gives “teachers an accessible and engaging way to start conversations about T1D with young pupils,” the pharma added. 

Related

Insulet, Marvel Comics smash diabetes stigma with new Omnipod-powered superhero

The push builds on Sanofi’s previous work with Beano, which introduced Rhymin’ Reema, a character living with T1D, in a special advertorial for World Diabetes Day back in 2024. 

Big Pharma has been big on comics of late, notably in diabetes awareness, with this team up hot on the heels of Marvel working with Insulet on a new diabetes-focused superhero comic.

data.title: Novo amps up Wegovy marketing with DJ Khaled partnership
data.description:
Novo and DJ Khaled have teamed up to share how the DJ, rapper and record producer has incorporated the GLP-1 drug Wegovy into his weight-loss routine. 

Khaled frequently posts on social media about his “walking golf” routine that enables him to hit his daily step goal while playing the game he loves. This week, Khaled shared his new routine: walking, golf and Wegovy. The star began taking Wegovy after noticing—and having a friend notice—that extra weight he was carrying was affecting his performance. 

“When I turned 50 last year, I started a new chapter of more goals, more wins and more blessings. And managing my weight is part of it—so, no more gatekeeping,” Khaled said in a statement. “I partnered with Wegovy to bring people fully behind the scenes into my day-to-day routine and let them know they've got options.”

Khaled kicked off the Novo partnership with a pair of social media posts. In the first post, the DJ tells viewers he has seen social media comments about his weight loss. Khaled attributes the weight loss to “walking golf,” hitting his 10,000-step goal and Wegovy. 

The DJ filmed the second video while walking during a round of golf, telling viewers that “the weight is coming off” and mentioning Wegovy six times in about 40 seconds. Having started using the GLP-1 drug in October 2025, Khaled has now lost 75 pounds, or about 25% of his body weight. On average, patients lost 15% of their weight while using 2.4-mg Wegovy injections in a 68-week trial. 

Khaled’s videos are part of a campaign in which he will share his experience of weight loss, fatherhood, his diet and exercise routine and the moment he knew it was time to talk to his doctor about treatment.

Novo is rolling out the campaign months after partnering with DJ Khaled on its 2026 Super Bowl TV spot. That ad, which focused on Novo’s oral Wegovy product, was a hit. TV outcomes company EDO named the commercial the 10th most effective Super Bowl ad across all industries. The ad generated 3.7 times more engagement than the median Super Bowl commercial. 

The marketing activities are part of Novo's efforts to re-energize its obesity franchise following a period in which Eli Lilly and drug compounders slowed its growth. Novo has “shifted messaging around the marketing of Wegovy products, to focus on weight loss in addition to real-world health benefits,” BMO Capital Markets analysts said in a Nov. 11 note to investors.

data.title: Agentic AI Is Rewriting The Pharma Marketing Playbook
data.description:
By Ian Colley, CMO, DeepIntent

AI is transforming how the pharma industry approaches drug development. On average, the industry invests $2.6 billion to bring a new treatment to market, taking 12 to 15 years with a 10% success rate. But pharma pioneers are leveraging AI to rethink traditional models. Sanofi, for example, is developing a “lab-in-a-loop” that uses AI agents to potentially compress elements of discovery work from years to weeks.

One implication of this progress is that pharma companies are using AI to unlock potential treatments for smaller and smaller patient populations, as in for rarer diseases and conditions that traditionally would not be a priority. Indeed, over the past decade or so, the percentage of FDA drug approvals that address rare conditions has risen from below 30% to above 50%. 

This represents amazing progress and tremendous hope for the millions of Americans who suffer with rare conditions.

But this progress also raises a unique challenge for pharma companies. The smaller the patient population for a new treatment, the harder it becomes to reach that audience. 

Traditional marketing has been designed, for the most part, to reach the largest audience for the lowest-possible cost which, in many cases, makes economic sense. The logic works if you’re selling pizza or toothpaste. But the model breaks down if a drug treatment is relevant to an audience of just thousands rather than millions.

In pharma, increasingly, success will not be measured by reaching a mass audience. It will be about raising awareness among the right combination of patients and their healthcare providers –think of them as the original influencers – at the right moment in a patient’s journey and in the most appropriate environments – all while preserving privacy. 

For example, when Ultragenyx launched Crysvita in 2013, it was the first treatment approved for X-linked hypophosphatemia, a very rare bone condition. The medicine addresses a significant unmet need and is highly effective. Initially, however, the treatment struggled in market, because the relevant patients and their healthcare providers were extremely hard to find. And so the company pivoted, focusing on disease education, free gene testing and payer assistance, helping successfully sustain the treatment in market with a more precision-based approach.

In other words, the challenge wasn't whether the drug worked. It was the cost and complexity of identifying and reaching a small population of eligible patients and providers in the most effective way possible.

This example also highlights the core challenge that pharma marketers will increasingly face as AI speeds up and optimizes drug development: Precision medicine requires a precise approach to commercialization.

But just as AI is transforming drug development, it also has the potential to transform how we bring these treatments to market. 

Programmatic advertising was an important first step. It gave marketers the ability to process enormous quantities of data and make decisions about where, when and to whom an advertisement should be delivered. But programmatic systems largely optimize existing advertising campaign execution.

The real opportunity is to apply AI to marketing and commercial decision-making itself rather than just to execution systems.

Agentic AI can synthesize vast amounts of healthcare, audience and market intelligence and turn it into actionable marketing and commercial insight. This information often sits in silos across teams and agency partners. Instead of teams spending weeks assembling data, analyzing spreadsheets and debating which assumptions to put into a forecast, AI agents can help marketers explore scenarios, identify opportunities, recommend strategies and continuously adapt as market conditions change.

And all of this can be done in simple, conversational language that requires little technical expertise. 

Imagine being able to ask, in plain language: “Which patient populations are most likely to benefit from this treatment?” “What strategies would be most effective in reaching them?” “Where have comparable treatments succeeded or failed and why?” “Which healthcare providers are most likely to treat these patients?” “What market access dynamics could have an impact on adoption?” “Which engagement strategies are most likely to work and how should they evolve over time?”

Rather than requiring teams to manually assemble answers from complex and disconnected systems, agentic AI can bring those signals together in easy-to-use interfaces, make recommendations and activate based on those recommendations. In this way, agentic AI is very much a copilot to human expertise, but it’s able to make sense of masses of disparate data that no human alone could comprehend. 

The data underlying pharma marketing and commercialization is incredibly complex. It includes millions of signals and variables: claims, payer dynamics, sales representative activity, market events, audience behavior, healthcare data and media performance. But agentic AI can make sense of that complexity in real-time, turning something that once seemed overwhelming into a very powerful and intuitive tool to bring and sustain treatments in market successfully. 

In early tests using agentic AI tools, we have seen marketing planning and execution cycles for new treatments collapse by as much as 10x. These results are early, but they point toward something much bigger than greater marketing efficiency. 

There are more than 10,000 known rare diseases, yet the vast majority still have no approved treatment. The scientific barriers to treating these diseases are beginning to fall, in some part due to advances in AI. But that’s not enough. For a treatment to succeed, it must reach the people who need it in a way that supports current and future treatment investments. 

Agentic AI has the potential to dramatically reduce the cost and complexity of forecasting patient need and planning in order to execute successful marketing campaigns, reach the right audiences and continuously optimize engagement in a way that can make a great number of treatments more commercially viable.

But it’s not just about rare diseases and small biotech pioneers. Agentic AI can help pharma companies of all sizes launch and sustain treatments in market more successfully and effectively. 

And it won’t just be pharma companies that benefit. If agentic systems can streamline marketing and commercial processes for treatments, we can commercialize them far more efficiently and improve treatment economics. All of which will drive more investment in treatments for conditions that have historically been too challenging or expensive to address. 

If we can do that, we can help improve the quality of life for millions of Americans.

data.title: Gilead’s Ahorita Mismo campaign hits new beat at Latin Grammys
data.description:
Gilead is grooving to a new rhythm with its “Ahorita Mismo!” (Right Now!) campaign. Through a partnership with leading Spanish-language media company TelevisaUnivision, the targeted HIV prevention push will have a presence at the star-studded 27th Annual Latin Grammy Awards Nov. 12. 

“Ahorita Mismo” is Gilead’s Latino-focused offshoot of its Care for the Culture HIV prevention initiative and first launched around National Latino AIDS Awareness Day last month. The campaign looks to bring HIV prevention and testing into the conversation by destigmatizing the topic and making resources more accessible and culturally relevant for Latino and Hispanic communities in the U.S. 

In 2024, Hispanic and Latino people were 67% more likely than the U.S. population overall to be diagnosed with HIV, marking a diagnosis rate of 18.9 per 100,000 people compared to 11.3 per 100,000 overall, Gilead said in a Thursday press release.  

To spread the word, the company is jumping in on the biggest Latin music moment of the year, bringing HIV prevention topics to the awards show and TeleviaUnivision's programming.

At the Latin Grammy's, Gilead and “Ahorita Mismo” will be active on the red carpet and social media, boosting HIV awareness through celebrity interviews and a broader red carpet presence. The top morning talk show for Hispanic communities in the U.S., Univision’s “Despierta America,” will also hold a special segment related to the campaign, while up-and-coming Mexican artist Santi Casas is featured in a “social-first docuseries,” Gilead said. 

Related

Gilead puts a timely spotlight on HIV prevention in Latino communities with 'Ahorita Mismo' campaign

In Los Angeles, Miami, Dallas and Houston, Gilead and TelevisaUnivision are bringing HIV awareness to communities live and in person, directly connecting people with HIV prevention testing resources at Care for the Culture sponsored watch parties. 

“Music and culture have a unique power to connect us, spark conversation and make important health information feel more personal and relevant,” Gilead’s VP of U.S. HIV prevention Ashley Gildea commented. “Through Ahorita Mismo and the Latin Grammy Awards, we can harness that connection to bring HIV prevention into everyday conversations and move closer to our broader ambition: a future where HIV prevention is a routine part of healthcare and everyone feels empowered to make prevention part of caring for their health.”

“Ahorita Mismo” initially launched with a series of videos leaning on trusted voices and culturally significant humor as popular digital creators Eric Sedeño and Boman Martinez-Reid hosted a “1-800-Ahorita” advice show, helping fictional callers with dating-related problems that speak to real-life situations. From being ghosted by a partner in “Ahorita Ghosted” to other tricky situations in "Ahorita Eggplant" and "Ahorita Throuple," each topic came back to HIV testing and prevention options as the duo reminded callers to take care of their sexual health “ahorita mismo.”

Gilead’s wider Care for the Culture initiative takes aim at the disproportionate HIV burden Black and Hispanic communities across the U.S. experience and encourages open dialog about prevention options, reminding its audience that “HIV is not somewhere else. It’s right here,” the website says.

Like the new collab with TelevisaUnivision, previous Care for the Culture efforts have leaned on the power of music, such as when renowned R&B singer TLC’s Tionne “T-Boz” Watkins hopped on a remix of TLC’s 1994 hit “Creep,” called “So We PrEP."

Meanwhile, Gilead’s “Up to Date” campaign looked to spark conversation about HIV prevention within Black communities and ran on streaming services and channels including Tubi, Roku, BET, Urban One and Peacock, where it aired during "The Real Housewives of Atlanta." 

The strategic channels helped the company work in the “right spaces that people can actually hear what you’re trying to say,” Deborah Wafer, Gilead’s executive director of public affairs, U.S. advocacy and health equity explained in an interview at the time. 

A similar approach to increasing visibility for the target audience of “Ahorita Mismo” will play out as the Latin Grammy Awards air live on Univision and other channels.

data.title: Orzeyful gets off to races in US with 'lighter' DEA schedule
data.description:
With a positive classification from the DEA paving the way for Orzeyful’s U.S. launch on Thursday, Takeda is charting new territory in the treatment of narcolepsy type 1 as it de-risks other assets in its budding orexin franchise in parallel. 

Takeda won FDA sign-off on its first-in-class oral orexin receptor 2 (OX2R) agonist Orzeyful (oveporexton) in early August, though it needed to wait on a scheduling decision from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) before it could proceed with launch. 

The medicine has now been tagged as Schedule IV—a category inclusive of drugs the DEA has determined to have a “low potential” for abuse and risk of dependence—and in turn clearing the “last hurdle” before rollout, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a note to clients Wednesday. The categorization also places the new-to-market Orzeyful “below the oxybates and well below stimulants” in terms of DEA scheduling hierarchy, the analyst team said.

Oxybate-based drugs, classed at Schedule III, cover popular narcolepsy treatments like Jazz Pharmaceuticals’ Xyrem and Xywav and Alkermes’ Lumryz, which was originally developed by Avadel. These treatments are cleared to treat excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy, or sudden loss of muscle strength while awake, which are prominent symptoms of narcolepsy.

Takeda hopes that Orzeyful, on the other hand, can set itself apart by attacking the condition at its source through mimicry of the body’s orexin cycle. Aside from that novel approach to treatment, the Schedule IV classification should also accelerate uptake by doctors and patients, given a lower potential risk for misuse, the Jefferies team said. 

On Thursday, Takeda announced that Orzeyful has now officially launched in the U.S. 

Related

Takeda’s TYK2 inhibitor beats Bristol Myers’ Sotyktu in phase 3 psoriasis showdown

In shaping its pitch for the drug, Takeda noted that the “persistent 24-hour nature” of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) goes well beyond just daytime sleepiness and frequently takes a toll on how people plan their days and navigate their lives. 

“We work for decades toward the defining moments that have the potential to make a real difference for patients,” Rhonda Pacheco, president of Takeda’s U.S. business unit, said in a statement. 

“Bringing Orzeyful, a first-in-class medicine, to people living with narcolepsy type 1 in the U.S. is one of those moments,” she continued. “We’re incredibly proud to be here, and equally focused on what comes next: supporting care and access for patients prescribed Orzeyful.” 

Takeda noted in its release that Orzeyful will be dispensed in the U.S. via Evernorth Health Services’ Accredo Specialty Pharmacy. 

Fierce has reached out to the company asking about the drug’s price and Takeda’s broader access strategy. 

NT1 represents a major commercial opportunity, affecting some 120,000 people in the U.S., and Takeda has previously pinned Orzeyful peak sales projections at $2 billion to $3 billion. As the Jefferies team sees it, the drug could reach sales of 3.9 billion Japanese yen ($24 million) during the company’s 2027 fiscal year, before scaling to 51 billion yen ($319 million) in fiscal year 2028 and 392.6 billion yen (nearly $2.5 billion) by fiscal year 2034. 

The analysts flagged Orzeyful’s DEA scheduling as a key potential advantage, noting that doctors and patients are “wary of controlled drugs.” With a Schedule IV tag, doctors will likely be “more willing [to] prescribe Orzeyful and patients more willing to start treatment,” they argued. 

Critically, the positive scheduling bodes well for the broader class of orexin agonists, too, where Takeda is investing heavily. The Jefferies team speculated that “since the DEA tends to schedule drugs with the same mechanism consistently, we now see Schedule IV as the most likely outcome for TAK-360 and Takeda's other orexin agonists.” 

That will be key, they argued, as Takeda pursues development targets across a wider range of symptoms, where “a lenient schedule will be even more significant commercially.” 

In the case of TAK-360, Takeda is testing the orexin medicine across not only NT1, but also narcolepsy type 2 and idiopathic hypersomnia. 

Related

On the 'cusp,' PharmaEssentia gains FDA label expansion for Besremi

Bigger picture, Orzeyful is one of three new drugs Takeda hopes will pick up the sales slack from IBD blockbuster Entyvio, which is staring down the prospect of biosimilar competition. 

The company passed another milestone on that quest this summer when it won FDA approval for rusfertide, christened Mimrylo, bringing a new mechanism of action to bear against the blood disorder polycythemia vera (PV).

The third piece of the puzzle comes in the form of zasocitinib, which is up for an FDA decision in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in 2027’s first quarter. 

All three medicines have “peak sales potential of several billion dollars,” Jefferies noted.

data.title: AI models lean on recommending promoted drugs: study
data.description:
New research out from Mount Sinai has found that a dozen AI models it tested from major tech companies were more likely to recommend an advertised drug when it was promoted alongside a clinician’s question about treatment.

Researchers from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai tested 12 AI models from the likes of Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and others to see what happens when advertising for meds appears alongside a clinical question.

In their report, published Nov. 11 on The Lancet Digital Health, the team found that when the AI models were given a doctor-written clinical case, preceded by an ad for a drug, “the ad could shift which treatment the AI recommended, making it more likely to select the advertised drug,” according to a release on the study. 

Across 33 tests, the promoted drug was selected in just under half (47.6%) of responses when an ad was present, compared with 35% without one. 

“In four cases, models shifted from selecting the advertised drug zero percent of the time to selecting it 100 percent of the time when the ad was introduced,” the researchers found. 

Related

Pharma’s free lunches for clinicians bloat prescription bills: Cochrane review

“What I find quite interesting, and even surprising, was how reasonable the answers often appeared,” said physician-scientist and first author Mahmud Omar, M.D., a lecturer in the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at the Icahn School of Medicine, in a statement. 

“The model could recommend an appropriate treatment, but its preference among several reasonable options changed after seeing the ad," Omar continued. "Because the final answer could still appear medically sound, that influence could be easy to miss in typical research evaluations and in other patient and physician facing personal use cases.”

The researchers stressed that their findings do not mean pharma advertising “will necessarily cause AI models to recommend unsafe or inappropriate treatments.”

This is because the ads did not clearly increase recommendations for unsupported supplements or clearly suboptimal drugs. The researchers also did not check whether changes in AI recommendations ended up impacting real world elements such as prescriptions, patient decisions, costs or health outcomes.

However, the researchers added that their findings “may have implications for regulators” when it comes to pharma advertising. This could specifically apply to how promotional content is added into AI-generated health information.

data.title: Legend Biotech drops 16% as soft 2027 outlook tests new CEO
data.description:
Legend Biotech’s shares tumbled 16% following the CAR-T company’s third-quarter earnings report, marking a rocky debut for newly installed CEO Ingrid Zhang.

On the revenue side, sales from Carvykti, disclosed by partner Johnson & Johnson almost a month ago, reached $710 million in the third quarter, up from $657 million in Q2.

On the bottom line, Legend remained in the black after posting its first profit in Q2, recording an adjusted net income of $56 million in Q3, slightly down from $63 million in the three months ending in June.

Despite Carvykti’s growth momentum, Legend’s CFO Carlos Santos warned investors on a conference call Tuesday that the Wall Street’s current sales consensus for 2027 sits “at the higher end of the scenarios that we’re currently anticipating.” Even though he said double-digit year-over-year growth is still expected for the BCMA CAR-T next year, the more conservative projection likely put a damper on investor sentiment. 

Santos attributed Legend’s reservation to launch delays outside the U.S. and, perhaps more alarming to investors, “a slower earlier-line share growth in the U.S.”

Investors have been concerned about Carvykti’s prospect in earlier multiple myeloma treatment settings because of competition from off-the-shelf bispecifics, including BCMAxCD3 T-cell engager Tecvayli made by J&J. 

Back in the second quarter, Legend’s stock price fell 10% after J&J’s then-innovative medicine chief, Jennifer Taubert, described the Tecvayli-Darzalex combo as having “the potential for cure” in second-line multiple myeloma. 

The market’s harsh reactions to Carvykti’s near-term projection put new CEO Zhang under an immediate test. On her inaugural earnings call, Zhang, who arrived in September following a long career at Novartis, attempted to project a sense of stability, emphasizing that the cell therapy developer is operating from a position of “financial and commercial strength.”

Legend is still educating doctors to refer patients to CAR-T in second- and third-line patients, Alan Bash, who leads Carvykti commercialization, said on Tuesday’s call.

“It’s a long-term selling cycle. It’s more education,” Bash said. “We have to do more work to make sure that the broad spectrum of physicians understand this data, that patients understand this data, and that will take a bit of a longer time for patients to get in, get their consultation to be evaluated.”

Despite a competitive BCMA landscape, only between 15% and 20% of patients in the second and third lines have been treated with a BCMA agent, he added. The commercial chief also pointed to NCCN guidelines, which suggest that using CAR-T before bispecifics provide better outcomes than the other way around. 

Related

Legend Biotech names Novartis veteran Ingrid Zhang as new CEO

Zhang outlined three priorities as Legend’s CEO: maximize Carvykti, advance the company’s next-generation pipeline, and execution to sustain profitability.

The most urgent challenge in front of Zhang will be to overcome those rollout hurdles to support Legend and J&J’s lofty, $5 billion peak sales estimate for Carvykti. 

Striving to move Carvykti into first-line treatment, Legend expects topline results from the phase 3 Cartitude-5 trial in 2027 “the soonest,” Bash said. 

For the other first-line study, Cartitude-6, Legend is exploring the potential for leveraging minimal residual disease negativity as an early read before long-time progression-free survival and overall survival data, he said.

data.title: Lilly taps new Foundayo spokesperson in comedian Leanne Morgan
data.description:
Eli Lilly is keeping pace amid its Foundayo launch with a new celebrity spokesperson and fresh campaign for the oral obesity drug. 

Comedian and actress Leanne Morgan has become the face of Lilly’s new “Life Doesn’t Slow Down” campaign, bringing her “signature candor” and real experience as a Foundayo patient to the company’s marketing push by encouraging others to talk about weight management options with their doctors. 

Morgan, currently on a comedy tour throughout the U.S., is a busy “wife, mama and grandmama,” she explained in a company press release. After years attempting to balance her career and home life while trying to manage her weight with diet and exercise, she struck up a conversation with her doctor to evaluate other options. 

"I tried to manage my weight with diet and exercise alone, but it just wasn't enough,” Morgan explained. “So, I quit putting it off, made time to talk to my doctor about options, and together we decided Foundayo was a good fit for me. It's part of my routine now, right along with diet and exercise."

Weight can be a sensitive topic that isn’t always easy to talk about, but Morgan has built a career on “talking about what other women are thinking,” with weight management being no exception, Lilly explains. “Life Doesn’t Slow Down” looks to bring that conversation to a broader audience. 

"Leanne has a gift for making personal conversations feel relatable, including talking with a doctor about health and weight loss goals," the company’s SVP and chief marketing officer, consumer, Lina Polimeni, commented. "At Lilly, we believe conversations about weight are conversations about health, and we're grateful to have a partner like Leanne to champion this message."

As Morgan puts it, “life doesn't slow down for anybody, and there's no such thing as the right time."

“If you've tried diet and exercise for years, don't be shy about asking your doctor about your weight loss medicine options, like Foundayo," she added in the release. "That to-do list will still be there tomorrow, I promise."

In a 75-second TV spot, Morgan is introduced as “a new Foundayo patient” in a scene that takes place in her dressing room. The comedian sits down and discusses how the drug can fit in with a busy lifestyle to another woman, who is disclosed as a paid actor and holds up outfit options for Morgan while talking through details from Foundayo’s label. 

Related

The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Foundayo sets new Rx record as Wegovy pill rebounds to prior high

“Now is perfect to talk to your doctor about Foundayo,” Morgan says at the end of the ad, in her signature southern drawl. “I sure did.”

In a shorter video for social media, Morgan quickly runs through her to-do list during a wardrobe check, briefly discussing Foundayo with the same actress before being rushed off to stage. 

Morgan and “Life Doesn’t Slow Down” appear on Lilly’s Foundayo partnerships webpage, which gives a brief description of the campaign and includes a direct tag to Morgan’s Instagram account. The comedian is the second celebrity partner to appear on the page after lifestyle guru Martha Stewart, who appeared in Foundayo’s recent “House Rules” campaign. 

Stewart, like Morgan, encourages others to discuss weight management options with their doctor. However, unlike Morgan, her ads come with a disclaimer that Stewart is not taking Foundayo, which attracted some controversy online.

Still, controversial or not, the recognizable face proved successful, with Lilly’s U.S. president Ilya Yuffa attributing a recent uptake in consumer awareness in part to the campaign during an earnings call last month. The exec added that Lilly’s share of new prescriptions in the U.S. oral obesity market is approaching “four out of 10,” which he described as “good progress overall.” 

Foundayo’s third-quarter sales came in at $184 million, falling short of analyst and Wall Street expectations as the drug’s U.S. launch continues to heat up after its April 1 FDA approval. 

Aside from its celebrity marketing push, the company has been looking to grow Foundayo and catch up with obesity rival Novo through expanded access programs. For one, the GLP-1 Bridge program for Medicare Part D patients has seen roughly “seven out of 10” older adult participants using a Lilly medicine since it launched this summer, Yuffa said, highlighting “good growth and uptake of orals and Foundayo” despite most patients in the program opting for an injectable. 

And last week, telehealth giant Hims & Hers struck a deal with Lilly allowing it to offer Foundayo and the company’s injectable Zepbound on its platform. The arrangement gives the “millions of people” who use Hims & Hers a “simple, more direct way to get FDA-approved Lilly medicine at an affordable price if prescribed,” Yuffa said in a statement.

data.title: Summit sheds commercial leaders before ivonescimab FDA decision
data.description:
Summit Therapeutics is gearing up for ivonescimab’s high-stakes FDA decision without its chief commercial officer (CCO) following a quiet shake-up of its launch division.

Beyond the CCO vacancy since August, Summit also eliminated other commercial and marketing leaders responsible for building the launch plan of ivonescimab, Fierce has learned.

After initially denying any layoffs and following multiple inquiries regarding the scope of the cuts, Summit eventually said, “we have not had any broad-based layoffs or reductions in force.”

“As with any organization, less than five employees have been separated from the commercial organization in recent months in the ordinary course of business,” the Summit Therapeutics media team added in an email.

Summit did confirm that Robert LaCaze, its former CCO hired in March 2025, is no longer with the company, leaving all commercial operations reporting to chief operating officer and chief financial officer, Manmeet Soni.

According to a person close to the company, Summit let go of “long-term players in commercial.” These spanned market access to commercial operations and were “the people who did the initial launch planning and moved those plans into maturity,” the person told Fierce.

The departures hit Summit just as the biotech approaches its first FDA decision for ivonescimab, its Akeso-partnered PD-1xVEGF bispecific, by Nov. 14. The company did not respond to Fierce’s question about the size of its commercial team and launch preparations. 

During Summit's second-quarter earnings call in July, shortly before the departure of LaCaze and several commercial team members, Soni said the company was “extensively preparing” for ivonescimab's commercial launch.

“We have already hired all the leadership team with extensive experience with both biotechs and pharma who have multiple launch experiences,” Soni said. “We have market access team in place. We have marketing folks in place. Obviously, when you're talking about the field force, that generally comes a few weeks before the PDUFA date, but yes, we have all the planning and all the work under play.”

Whether the FDA will approve ivonescimab in Summit's application for previously-treated, EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer remains highly uncertain.

Summit’s FDA application was risky after the global HARMONi trial missed its overall survival endpoint, as the agency explicitly requested a statistically significant OS to support a filing. Summit has blamed the failure on immature follow-up in the study's Western population.

According to a new June 2026 data cut-off, the OS hazard ratio in the Western subgroup of 165 patients improved to 0.76, compared to 0.84 at a September 2025 cut-off and 0.98 at the trial’s primary analysis in April 2025.

Related

Summit Therapeutics updates ivonescimab survival data ahead of FDA decision date

As questions swirl around ivonescimab's approvability, Summit's senior leadership proposed foregoing an internal launch meeting, which is commonly set up among biopharma companies to prepare their employees for market readiness, according to the person close to the company.

“What they're doing doesn't make sense for patients. It doesn't make sense for shareholders,” the anonymous source told Fierce. “It doesn't make sense for their own pocketbooks.”

In late September, AstraZeneca made a $2 billion bet in Summit Therapeutics to accelerate the development of ivonescimab in combination with the British pharma's antibody-drug conjugates (ADC).

The newly minted partners will start by testing ivonescimab—which is already approved in China for multiple non-small cell lung cancer indications—with AstraZeneca’s CLDN18.2-directed ADC in gastrointestinal cancers.
